what: Adversarial refutation of Session C's own acceptance claims. Ten skeptics were told to REFUTE, not confirm; every non-HOLDS finding was then given to a second agent told to show the first was wrong.
head: ad1585f1
caveat: THE REFUTATION IS ITSELF FALLIBLE AND WAS SPOT-CHECKED. At least one CONFIRMED_BROKEN finding is wrong on its facts (the Q5 2/3-vs-0/3 measurement IS supported by two stored comparison records), and at least one was stale (it read gate record 24 and called 14-of-14 false, where record 25 is green). Findings are recorded as raised, not as adjudicated truth.

findings.claim: (6) 'Live references changed, records left alone. Inclusion rule: change a reference only if it is an ADDRESS used to reach the repository today; leave it if it is a RECORD of something that happened. 8 changed ... 19 left' — and the commit subject 'the repo rename reaches every live reference'.
findings.matters: Five live ADDRESSES in four files were missed by the sweep whose stated inclusion rule is exactly 'an address used to reach the repository today'. None is a captured log, fixture, dated provenance, ledger entry or generated view — the five categories the audit lists as the 19 deliberately left. `pnpm main:green` — the instrument this project uses to decide whether main is green before a merge — resolves its GitHub API path through the OLD name and only works because GitHub honours a rename redirect. That redirect is forfeited the moment any repository named `SeanJ22/we-the-people` exists again, at which point the green/red gate answers about a repository that is not this one. There is no test anywhere in the repo that pins the repository slug (`git grep` for a rename guard over tests/ returns only product-branding `we-the-people` UA assertions), so nothing would notice.

findings.claim: (2) '...every allowlisted file is checked for the one thing the guard actually exists to prevent: a bare origin literal, which is what a call site looks like' — the extra assertion proves each allowlisted file holds no bare origin literal.
findings.matters: This is the session's own failure pattern: an instrument that reports clean while looking past the thing it exists to catch. The regex requires the closing quote to follow the host with at most one slash, so it matches a bare origin and nothing else — a URL WITH A PATH, which is what an actual call site looks like, evades it entirely. Because the first sweep test allowlists the file by name, BOTH origins tests stay green with a real `fetch("https://meanwhileusa.com/api/build")` sitting inside `lib/governance/adoptions.ts` or `lib/tracker/registry.mjs`. The stated purpose of the second assertion — 'the failure mode is not the first entry, it is the fourth, added because the third was there' — is not achieved: the allowlist is still effectively 'trust me'.

findings.claim: (1, second half) tests/origins.test.ts enforces this.
findings.matters: middleware.ts is the ONE file in the repository whose entire job is routing by hostname — `isAdminHostRequest(request.headers, ADMIN_ORIGIN)` at line 90 — and it is the file most likely to acquire a hardcoded host. It sits outside every path the guard looks at, along with drizzle.config.ts, eslint.config.mjs, postcss.config.mjs, states/, public/, data/ and all of docs/. It currently imports ADMIN_ORIGIN correctly, so the FACT holds; the ENFORCEMENT does not extend to it, and the audit row cites the test as though it did. `--untracked` also does not cover gitignored files.

findings.claim: 'tests/origins.test.ts — six tests — for Item F ... tests 4561 ... That is 4,555 + 6'
findings.matters: Correct at the anchor the package names (35afd378) and stale at the head it ships from: 99bb8bec added the seventh test — the 'an allowlisted file holds PROSE' assertion that claim (2) rests on. The 4,555 + 6 = 4,561 arithmetic is presented as the thing that makes the suite total derivable, and it no longer derives the current head's total.

findings.claim: Item C: '...and every claim names a place to verify.' (the second half of the same claim)
findings.matters: This is the session's own established failure mode one level down: the citation resolves to a file, so it looks checked, but the file contains none of the numbers quoted from it — and the file it names is the very class of record ('suiteTotals: null on a PASS') the section is claiming to have fixed. An owner following the pointer reads a record that refutes the sentence pointing at it.

findings.claim: Item C: 'The Item-5 denominator table is derived, with the command beside it | The six tables above, each with its `node -e` one-liner. Re-run any of them | MET' — and the section header 'Every number in the six tables below was re-derived by running the command printed beneath it. None came from prose.'
findings.matters: The document contradicts itself: Item A on the same page states 'The candidate universe moved 55 → 266' and 'the registry equals the corpus — 268', while Item 5 prints AZ 55 and 57. The acceptance row that says the tables ARE derived is the exact claim that fails, and it fails in the direction that most understates the gap: the AZ known-vs-canonical shortfall is presented as 2 candidates when it is 213. The commands were printed but not re-run — 'None came from prose' is itself prose.

findings.claim: Item 5 caveat: 'Each state is currently derived from exactly one certified pilot-county ballot — `data/states/az/ballot/az-pima-2026.json`, `nh-merrimack-2026.json`, `nj-morris-2026.json`.'
findings.matters: The caveat is the sentence that tells the owner how far to trust every number under it. Stated as written it understates Arizona's acquisition, contradicting Item A of the same package, which correctly reports the SOS acquisition as MET.

findings.claim: Item C: 'The gate record persists suite totals on a PASSING run' — verify with `scripts/gates.mjs` and `node -e '...require("./data/ops/gate-runs/<newest>.json")...suiteTotals'` — MET.
findings.matters: The claim is true of the code and false of the pointer. An owner told to 'check the newest gate-run file' gets a FAIL record today, and the record the close names by hand (09) is one of the ABSENT ones. Two of the three cited routes to this claim land on evidence that does not show what is claimed.

findings.claim: Item C, final row: 'Every generated artifact regenerated, `pnpm handoff --check` green' — verified by '`pnpm regen` prints `STALE 0`; `pnpm handoff --check`', result 'See the close of this document' (which reports `CURRENT 37 · STALE 0` and `pnpm gates` 14 of 14 green).
findings.matters: This is the one row in Item C whose result cell defers to prose elsewhere in the same document rather than to a record. The record that does exist at HEAD disagrees with that prose. Whether the failure is a real generator drift or the Windows concurrency race the staged test comment argues for, the acceptance is not currently demonstrable — and it is the row that gates 'every generated artifact regenerated', which is RULING 92 and RULING 102 law.

findings.claim: 'RouteTask dispositions 301' (docs/owner-audit/session-c.md line 636, in the row whose 'Where to verify' is data/health/control-plane-readback/2026-09-01-03.json)
findings.matters: The audit names one file as the place to verify and then reports a number that file does not contain. A reader who opens the cited artifact finds 342 where the table says 301 — the audit's own verification instruction refutes its own number. The by-verdict breakdown moved too (230 -> 266 REQUIRES_NEW_ADAPTER between -02 and -03), so this is a stale copy from an earlier run, not a typo.

findings.claim: 'there is no path by which a count reaches the artifact without the reader having printed it' (audit line 635, repeated verbatim in the artifact's own _note)
findings.matters: The sentence is doing the work of a guard while no guard exists. 'There is no path' reads as a checked invariant; it is an assertion in a comment. Any later hand edit, or a regenerate against a modified reader, lands undetected — the same class as a green suite that hides a deleted test.

findings.claim: Implied by (1): the parse is strict, so an artifact that lands is an artifact whose counts were all read out of the reader's output
findings.matters: This is precisely the failure pattern the audit is supposed to be hunting: an instrument reporting a clean result while looking at nothing. `byRecordClass: {}` and `dispositionsByVerdict: {}` in a landed artifact are indistinguishable from 'the control plane holds no record classes' — an absence asserted about our own store from a parse miss. The header's contrast between the strict obligations guard ('a FAILED read... never an empty store') and the seven unguarded fields shows the author knew the shape and applied it to one field.

findings.claim: Sub-claim the audit endorses by pointing at the artifact's _note: moving the class needs 'a run whose runClass is CI or SCHEDULED (set by the environment, not by a flag)'
findings.matters: The audit's argument for why Item E is honest rests on the runClass clause being environmental rather than assertable. It is assertable. The safety in this specific record comes from the integration clause, not the one the audit names — and a future run on an already-merged clean SHA would need only `WTP_RUN_CLASS=CI` to award itself INDEPENDENTLY_REPRODUCED, which is the exact label RULING 216 retired.

findings.claim: 'instrumentWritesNothing: true' in the artifact records that the read-back instrument writes nothing
findings.matters: The field asserts a property of a DIFFERENT file, in a JSON record, with no instrument behind it. It is true today by inspection and false the moment anyone adds an output path to the reader — and the artifact would go on saying true. A field a model fills in about its own instrument is the shape RULING 216 was written against.

findings.claim: Implied by Item E's framing: the artifact is a current reading of the shipped head
findings.matters: Structurally unavoidable rather than dishonest: readRunProvenance runs BEFORE writeFileSync, so a clean-tree reading is dirtied by the act of recording it, and the recorded SHA is always the parent of the commit that contains it. Worth naming because it means workingTreeClean:true can never coexist with the artifact being committed at the SHA it names — the strongest reachable state for this instrument is a CI re-run, exactly as the _note says.

findings.claim: Audit Item B, 'Where to verify': "Run it against a local production build: `pnpm build && pnpm start`, then `node --test --experimental-strip-types --import ./scripts/register-test-loader.mjs tests/new-zip-render.test.ts`" — producing the stated Result "MET — 18 contests, 19 candidate cards, 0 browser outbound, 0 server outbound."
findings.matters: The audit's stated instrument cannot produce the audit's stated result. An owner following Item B verbatim gets a SKIP and an exit code of 0, which in a suite summary is indistinguishable from the check having been satisfied.

findings.claim: Item B Result: "MET — 18 contests, 19 candidate cards, 0 browser outbound, 0 server outbound."
findings.matters: The only evidence for the numbers is the sentence asserting them. Nothing in the repository — no log, no diagnostic capture, no gate record — records that the render ever happened, and the check cannot be re-run without a build.

findings.claim: "Outbound acquisition is trapped at BOTH layers ... Server: scripts/trap-outbound.mjs ... wraps fetch, http.request/get and https.request/get" — presented as covering "a route handler hunting during SSR".
findings.matters: The audit presents the server layer as closing the SSR hole. The one escalation rung this codebase actually uses to defeat blocks is invisible to the trap, so "0 server outbound" is evidence about two clients in one process, not about packets leaving the machine.

findings.claim: Claim (3) implies the guard refuses to run unless the server-side trap is actually installed in the process being rendered ("an absent file means the preload never ran in the server process").
findings.matters: Start the server with the audit's own `pnpm start` (untrapped), point WTP_OUTBOUND_LOG at a log made this way, and the guard passes, the log stays empty, and the test asserts `after` deepEqual `[]` and reports '0 server outbound' over a server with no trap in it at all. That is precisely the session's established failure pattern: a clean report from an instrument looking at nothing.

findings.claim: The server trap is a working instrument (implied by reporting '0 server outbound' as a measured result).
findings.matters: Combined with the guard hole above, nothing in the repository can distinguish a functioning server trap from a no-op. A wrapper that failed to install, or was replaced later in the server's startup, would produce exactly the observed 'empty log' and be read as proof of a clean render.

findings.claim: Item B, read under RULING 229/224, that the render shows a reader at a new ZIP getting this session's held statewide records.
findings.matters: The render proves the August pilot ballot file projects onto a ZIP outside the pilot. It does not show that Item A's 266-candidacy corpus or the 268-row registry reaches any reader, which is what 'acquisition without promotion is inventory' asks.

findings.claim: '0 server outbound' as a measurement of the SSR render path.
findings.matters: Even a perfectly installed server trap could not have fired on this render, because nothing on the path can make a request. The run therefore demonstrates no discrimination: a working trap and a dead trap produce the identical empty log, and the audit reports the empty log as a positive result.

findings.claim: (5) "...and tests/brand-identity.test.ts guards it with a plant-check both ways."
findings.matters: "Plant-check both ways" is the specific reassurance that a guard is not a tautology. There is no red arm at all, so the file cannot distinguish "the rule holds" from "the sweep looked at nothing" — the exact failure mode this session already hit four times. The claim of a plant-check is itself unsupported.

findings.claim: (1)/(5) "--mark is referenced ONLY by the logo component" — guarded by the --mark scope test.
findings.matters: The scoping rule's stated purpose (globals.css:65-75) is that --mark must never appear where a reader could read it as a tier claim — legend dots are precisely where tier colours are LEARNED. A planted `.legend-dot[data-tier="state"] { fill: var(--mark); }` makes the brand assert "state government" and the guard says nothing. The claim that the token is guarded to the lockup is not what the code enforces.

findings.claim: (5) The undeclared-token sweep guards the class, including the eighteenth reference (the Tailwind-compiled comment).
findings.matters: The session found a defect caused by comments being compiled, wrote that lesson into the commit message, then built a guard that strips comments and skips the directory the defect was in. Reintroducing the identical defect passes every gate. The audit presents this class as "swept rather than patched"; the sweep does not cover the case that made it notable.

findings.claim: (5) "The undeclared-token sweep found and fixed 18 references" — i.e. 18 var() references that resolved to nothing.
findings.matters: 18 is a correct count of references touched, but the audit frames all of them as the class "that had ten border declarations painting nothing at all." Three of the eighteen did not paint nothing, and two of those three are explicitly excluded from the guard now cited as protecting the class. The number and the characterisation do not describe the same set.

findings.claim: (5) "Verified in a browser before and after" for the undeclared-border fixes.
findings.matters: The artifact is honest — it records found:false rather than inventing a reading — but the audit generalises one measured selector into "verified in a browser." Four of the five surfaces the commit names as fixed have no browser evidence in the package, and the reader cannot tell that from the row.

findings.claim: (2) "EB Garamond loads via next/font/google (self-hosted) and NO request reaches fonts.googleapis.com or fonts.gstatic.com" — backed by "Network capture: 344 requests, exactly two hosts."
findings.matters: The one number the audit offers as the RULING-159 floor is the one number the artifact does not persist, so the claim's own stated safeguard cannot be re-derived from the repo — a reader must take "344" on trust. The underlying no-Google-host result is nonetheless true and I reproduced it from the built output, which is stronger evidence than the prose. Note also that next/font/google DOES fetch from Google at BUILD time; the claim is only true of readers, which the audit's own row scopes correctly and the summary claim does not.

findings.claim: (1)/(5) The six sidebar captures at docs/evidence/brand-2026-09-01/after/sidebar-{dark,light}-{local,state,national}.png are where the owner settles the open dark-adjacency decision.
findings.matters: This is the one Item J row the audit marks OPEN — owner decision, and it is the only row where the owner's own eyes are the instrument. The package sends him to six files that are not in the repository, are excluded by .gitignore, and are not on disk in this worktree. He cannot make the decision the package asks him to make.

findings.claim: (1) The scoping rule on --mark is enforced by a named test.
findings.matters: The scoping comment the audit offers as proof of the rule cites a test file that does not exist — the repo's own recorded "a cited check may name nothing" pattern. The rule is in fact partially enforced by tests/brand-identity.test.ts, but a future session grepping for the named file finds nothing and cannot tell whether the guard was deleted or never written.

findings.claim: (1) "--font-record and --mark are declared dark-first in app/globals.css with the scoping comment."
findings.matters: Two tokens are described as sharing a declaration pattern and a comment that only one of them has, and the one that is NOT dark-first sits in the block this repo has already been burned by. The outcome is fine today — I confirmed both emit in the built chunk — but the guard asserts stylesheet text where the recorded lesson is to assert getComputedStyle, so it would stay green through the failure it is named for.

findings.claim: (6) "The map pin is removed from BOTH surfaces and --link is on no brand element."
findings.matters: The pin work is genuinely done and genuinely measured — that half is the strongest evidence in Item J. But ".brand-change" still wears --link (defensibly, it is a control), so the claim as written is false on its face and true only under an unstated definition of "brand element." More importantly, every invariant in claim (6) and the 18px floor in claim (3) is enforced by nothing: a later edit restoring the pin, re-tinting the lockup with --link, or deleting the wordmark floor leaves all 7 brand tests green.

findings.claim: (1) lib/ask/model.ts declares ASK_SYNTHESIS_MODEL = "claude-opus-5" and it is the ONLY place a model id is declared for Ask.
findings.matters: The precise property that makes rollback a one-line edit is "one declaration". Five ungoverned model-id literals sit one file over in the same directory, and one of them is dispatched as a live API arm. A reader taking "only place" literally would not know to check them when the model moves again.

findings.claim: (3) tests/ask-model-constant.test.ts refuses a module-bound binding, and it strips block comments so a file may explain the defect without tripping the guard.
findings.matters: The guard was written to close the exact defect this session just found, and it closes one spelling of it. The most likely future regression — dropping the arrow from `const askModel = (): string => resolveAskModel()` — is the case it cannot see. It also false-positives on a `//` line comment, which invites the next session to loosen rather than tighten it.

findings.claim: (3, companion instrument) tests/ask-model-economics.test.ts asserts that every Ask call site "must read the shared model constant".
findings.matters: This is the session's own named failure pattern — an instrument reporting clean while looking at nothing. Two guards now disagree about the same comment: ask-model-constant.test.ts strips it so the code can explain itself, and ask-model-economics.test.ts goes RED if it is ever deleted from correct code. Case E is the trap: a future cleanup that removes stale prose fails a test whose message accuses the code.

findings.claim: (7) derive() carries incomparable questions as unmeasured rather than filtering them out, so a vacuous SWITCH is impossible.
findings.matters: The repair closed the rows-level filter and left the template-level `continue` open, so the denominator can still shrink before the guard can see it. A checkout where the division index does not resolve the pilot ZIPs — which is a fact about the checkout, not about the models — would silently produce a SWITCH verdict over a handful of questions while `voided` sat in the record explaining why, unread by the rule.

findings.claim: (1) docs/state.md's new entry leads in READER TERMS and does not inflate — 'Ask answers are written by claude-sonnet-5, and on the two hardest canonical questions a reader gets an answer where they previously got none.'
findings.matters: The canonical session record's reader-facing lead asserts a product change that the same session reverted two commits later. The audit package gets this right (line 741: 'THE SWITCH WAS REVERTED THE SAME DAY ... lib/ask/model.ts reads claude-opus-5'), so the two session-owned documents now contradict each other, and the one an owner is told is canonical is the wrong one.

findings.claim: (1) The audit package docs/owner-audit/session-c.md says plainly that 211 acquired Arizona candidates reach NO reader surface, and calls it a defect under RULING 224.
findings.matters: The claim is half true: state.md line 22915 and frontier line 763 both state the defect squarely. The audit package — the document explicitly written 'for you, not for a machine' and the one the owner is pointed at — omits it entirely and marks the acquisition MET. Under RULING 224 an acquisition obligation does not close at the vault, so 'MET' with no promotion tail is the exact inflation the mandate names.

findings.claim: (1) '...on the two hardest canonical questions a reader gets an answer where they previously got none' / audit Item K: 'Sonnet held ... strictly more on both contested ones — Q3 1/3 vs 0/3, Q5 2/3 vs 0/3.'
findings.matters: 'Q5 2/3 vs 0/3' has no support in any stored measurement — every record has Q5 NOT_EVALUABLE 3/3 on BOTH arms, i.e. a reader gets no answer on either model. The frontier says so in as many words ('Q3 and Q5 fail identically on both models ... a real unanswered reader question'), directly contradicting both state.md's reader lead and audit Item K. Q3's best recent record is 1 of 3 passes, which is not 'a reader gets an answer'.

findings.claim: (1) docs/state.md's new entry LEADS in reader terms (RULING 225: infrastructure counts come afterward).
findings.matters: RULING 225 requires the report to lead with what a reader can now see, with infrastructure counts afterward. The entry's thesis sentence and the paragraph that follows it are both infrastructure, and the second is literally an infrastructure count (6 workstreams / 12 pairs / 0 serialized), placed ahead of the reader section. The audit package does order it correctly (its first section, line 36, is 'What a reader can now see'), so this is state.md only.

findings.claim: (2, extension) The frontier names THREE instruments that looked at nothing, and that is the session's full pattern.
findings.matters: The frontier is the artifact a later session inherits, and it under-counts the pattern it exists to carry. An override that reached one of four rungs while the tests stayed green is the same failure mode as the three that are listed — and the audit says outright it was found by hand rather than by an instrument.

findings.claim: (6) NS12 was auto-resolved by a real predicate reading a committed artifact, and it moved to docs/tracker-resolved.csv.
findings.matters: This is the dimension's failure pattern inside the fix built to end it. The predicate accepts four literal 'x' strings as proof a Netlify credential resolved; it will return RESOLVED_BY_EVIDENCE on every future run, on any machine including CI, forever, because the artifact is static and self-produced. So the row can never re-open by machine if the credential disappears — the artifact's own notes concede that re-opening depends on a later session recording it. That is the same 'nothing ever re-asks' defect the session says it removed, moved one level down.

findings.claim: state.md's closing numbers: 'suite 4,675 tests · 4,674 pass · 1 skipped' and 'gates 14 of 14'.
findings.matters: The session's canonical numbers block reports a green gate set at a head where the two most recent recorded gate runs both fail the test gate at 13 of 14. The audit package is more honest here — it cites its green run by id and SHA and tells the owner to read the newest record 'whatever it is' — but that instruction, executed, returns FAIL. (The session appears to be still working this: HEAD moved to 066f6c4c 'Re-run a RULING 92 mismatch before believing it, and name the race when it is one' during this audit, and no gate record exists for that SHA.)

findings.claim: Audit Item 4: '378 open, 69 Needs Sean, sections summing to 378 | docs/tracker.md — "378 open, 477 resolved"'
findings.matters: The audit's verification pointer is a quotation of a generated file, and the quotation does not match the file — both numbers are wrong (387→378, 478→477). state.md's own block gets it right ('478 resolved'). A 'where to check it' line that misquotes its target is the prose form of an instrument that reports without looking, and it is in the one document written to make the owner not take the session's word for anything.

findings.claim: state.md's 'The rulings' paragraph enumerates the session's rulings (232, 233, 234, 235).
findings.matters: RULING 236 is in the canonical ledger and is the record of the Ask-model revert. The session entry that explicitly enumerates 'The rulings' omits it, and so does the frontier — the same staleness that leaves the state.md reader lead claiming Sonnet 5 is serving readers.

findings.claim: (2, the rationale) '...because a session does not legislate' — i.e. the validator would have REFUSED a LAW_DECISION with session provenance.
findings.matters: This is the session's own failure pattern in governance form: a guard that reports clean can be looking at a field the writer controls. The 'a session does not legislate' invariant is enforced against the label, and not at all against amendment-by-FACT — so the discipline shown in 235/236 is authorship, not architecture, and the next session gets no help from the validator.

findings.claim: (3) RULING 233 deliberately claims NOTHING, and shipping.promotion_path is answered by RULING 1 with 'integrated-head-merges-to-main'.
findings.matters: The reader is told a declared question is answered by a standing law. In fact a 2026-09-01 session attached a value to a 2026-08-19 record whose text does not say it, and the only instrument that would have noticed the slot being empty is a hand-run script outside gates and CI. Governance:check would stay green with the slot unanswered.

findings.claim: Package instruction: 'Verify with pnpm governance:check at the integrated head, and pnpm governance:open --task meta-governance to read them' (docs/owner-audit/session-c.md:754).
findings.matters: The owner is handed a command that will not show him the records the row is about, and the two measurements this session most wants believed — the staging branch-name conflict and the model revert — are reachable only through the history view CLAUDE.md deliberately keeps out of default session context.

findings.claim: Incidental, found while parsing: the provenance routingNote on the session's own records.
findings.matters: The ledger's only free-text provenance field states, on record, that a measurement taken on 2026-09-01 by Session C was adopted by a brief six days earlier. It is the one field a later session would read to answer 'who asked for this?', and for 65 records it answers wrong.

findings.claim: 266 was 'established TWICE by independent mechanisms ... the two mechanisms share nothing, which is why their agreement is evidence' (corpus `extraction.method`, and the audit's Arizona row).
findings.matters: The audit sells 'two mechanisms that share nothing' as the reason a partial parse cannot pass as a complete corpus. The shared layer is precisely the one that silently drops rows, and nothing in the adapter or the 11-test file compares against `doc.numPages`. The next document parsed this way gets no such protection, and 266 held by measurement rather than by the guard.

findings.claim: (Your question: could population-label.ts return a WRONG label?) Implicit in the audit's 'MET' on labelling.
findings.matters: The guard that is supposed to stop a population inheriting a word it did not earn has a register entry that contradicts its own definitions and no test that would notice. It is right today by an accident of derivedFrom bookkeeping.

findings.claim: 'R-C9 labels corrected everywhere — MET, 9 sites found, 6 corrected by the lane, 3 corrected by the integration owner', cited to `git grep -n "statewide" -- lib scripts`.
findings.matters: This is the one Item A row whose evidence pointer is unusable. A reader running the command the audit names gets 365 lines and no way to reach 9 or to confirm 'everywhere'.

findings.claim: 'Enrichment obligations, with denominators — MET, 1,087 -> 1,720. AZ 795 against a denominator of 266 corpus candidacies; NH 114 against 47 pilot-derived; NJ 811 against 276 pilot-derived', cited to `pnpm readback:control-plane`.
findings.matters: A reader running the cited command gets 1,720 and no way to check the three numbers the row actually rests on, or to confirm that 925 of them stand over pilot-derived populations.

findings.claim: (1) — the enforcement surface. middleware.ts's own comment says the matcher 'cannot be narrowed to /admin/* ... would silently drop rule 1 the moment somebody optimised it, which is why the reasoning is written here next to the pattern.'
findings.matters: Whether middleware RUNS on `/api/admin/*` for a given host is decided by `config.matcher`, and nothing checks it. Replace the matcher with the Next.js docs' common default `["/((?!api|_next/static).*)"]` and `/api/admin/decision` on the public host would bypass middleware entirely — and every one of the 33 tests would still be green, because they invoke the function rather than the route. The reasoning that this must not happen is a comment, not a guard. This is the failure pattern named in the brief: the instrument does not look at the thing that actually enforces the rule.

findings.claim: (2) Seeded failure 2 — 'Unauthenticated requests on the admin host are refused': admin host /admin -> 307 to /admin/login?why=NOT_CONFIGURED; /api/admin/decision -> 401. Test names include 'a FORGED session cookie is refused on the admin host'.
findings.matters: In the suite as it actually runs, the HMAC verification code never executes. The 'FORGED session cookie is refused' test passes on a short-circuit that fires before any cryptography, and its regex was written wide enough to accept exactly that. Delete the entire `crypto.subtle.verify` block and the test stays green. The property itself is real — I proved BAD_SIGNATURE by supplying a key — but the audit's cited instrument does not prove it. Same for the 401: it is a NOT_CONFIGURED 401, not a no-session 401. The audit even quotes `why=NOT_CONFIGURED` as the evidence of success without noting that NOT_CONFIGURED means the check was never reached.

findings.claim: (2) Seeded failure 3 — 'A number rendered without a denominator fails the page's own check', evidenced by tests/admin-control-centre.test.ts and 'the render audit'. lib/control-plane/owner-surface.ts's doc comment: 'A number computed inline in the page — the exact way this rule gets broken — is caught here and nowhere else.'
findings.matters: An inline number is caught only if a human remembers to push it into the array — which is the exact discipline the check was written to replace. The ZIP grid renders `3 / 1 / 0` with no denominator on every row and `numberAudit.ok` is true. The seeded failure proves the FUNCTION rejects a null denominator; it does not prove the PAGE feeds it the numbers it renders, and the page demonstrably does not.

findings.claim: (2) — the page runs its own render audit before showing anything.
findings.matters: A vacuous green with self-congratulatory wording, printed at the foot of the page (line 519 renders `numberAudit.detail`). The state in which the page has no snapshot is precisely the state in which the owner most needs to be told nothing was checked, and instead he is told everything checked out.

findings.claim: (2) — the page's second self-check: 'every stated N equals the number of rows actually rendered'. owner-surface.ts: 'the two numbers come from different places, so only comparing the ACTUAL rendered row count can catch a divergence.'
findings.matters: `x !== x` is false for every finite x. This check cannot fail for any snapshot, ever. It is the same defect class the brief lists — an instrument reporting clean because it compares a value with itself. Its own doc comment states the opposite of what the code does. And the page's actual headline counts that a divergence could appear in (`Decisions recorded — {decisionsOut.value.length}` at line 409) are not in the claim list at all.

findings.claim: (5) 'pnpm promote:staging — eligible run exits 0 PROMOTION ELIGIBLE; refused run collects 7 refusals by name (STALE_HEAD, SUITE_RED, VISUAL_RED, REQUIRED_CHECKS_NOT_GREEN, WRONG_DATABASE, FREEZE_NOT_CLEAR, NOT_FAST_FORWARD) and exits 1; no flags exits 2.'
findings.matters: Neither cited run is reproducible by the command the audit names, because no gate record and no staging ref exist in the tree, and no artifact of those runs was committed. The '7 refusals' figure matches neither the live run (2) nor the unit test (9); it came from an ad-hoc hand-fed record that no longer exists. 'no flags exits 2' also mis-attributes cause: the code is `verdict.eligible ? 0 : couldNotTell ? 2 : 1` — the 2 comes from an unmeasurable head, not from the absence of flags. The refusal VOCABULARY is well tested at the pure-function level; the SCRIPT run quoted as evidence is not checkable.

findings.claim: (7) Netlify: domain_aliases contains admin.meanwhileusa.com, allowed_branches is ["main","test"], and the wildcard cert covers both. (Audit also asserts the certificate 'did not re-issue', re-read after the alias and branch-suffix changes.)
findings.matters: The three parts I was asked to check all hold and I confirmed them at the provider and over the wire: the alias is registered, allowed_branches is exactly [main, test], and the wildcard covers admin. and test. alike. The adjacent sub-claim in the same table row — that the certificate 'did not re-issue' — is contradicted by the object's own timestamps, and in any case is unprovable from a single reading with no recorded baseline. It is the audit's only cert claim that asserts a NON-event, and it is the one the evidence points against.
